While existing defenses have concentrated primarily on poisoning attacks, the vulnerabilities inherent in backdoors remain insufficiently addressed. This work introduces a defensive strategy designed to neutralize in-data- backdoor insertions into cloud-based services, ensuring that the resulting models are free of such hidden functionalities. Our approach operates without requiring changes to the service provider's training methods or access to clean reference labels. Furthermore, it functions independently of whether the attacker possesses knowledge of the activation trigger. By keeping both the trigger and label hidden while guaranteeing that the delivered service maintains equivalent performance to the original, we ensure a clean outcome for the backdoor's infiltrator. Numerical simulations demonstrate that this method not only infiltrates the model effectively but also successfully implants the intended triggers and labels into the trained network, ensuring the attacker's objectives are met.

Utilizing external knowledge to assist machine-based question answering (QA) on tasks requiring commonsense background faces the challenge of overwhelming and misleading information due to the boundless volume of such data. To address this, we introduce a semantics-driven, knowledge-aware QA framework designed to regulate knowledge injection from coarse to fine granularity. We implement a filtering strategy to refine extracted information based on the initial (coarse) semantics of a question and have created a semantics-aware retrieval module. This module leverages structural knowledge inputs and performs hierarchical fusion of appropriate facts aligned with the precise (fine-grained) semantics of questions. Experimental results indicate that our proposed method outperforms strong baseline approaches on the CommonsenseQA benchmark dataset.

This work addresses the challenge where a parameterized model must be trained across a network of data nodes, with each individual contributing a distinct data set. While the model owner holds the responsibility of parametric training, the raw data remains private and is shared only in privacy-preserving fashion. Although this setup constitutes the essence of Federated Learning (FL), it is frequently hindered by communication constraints and the fact that some nodes are slow or offline, causing them to fall behind in updates. These lagging nodes eventually fall so far behind that their contributions become insignificant, a phenomenon known as "staleness," which degrades model accuracy. We observe that these communication limits and the heterogeneous, often unbalanced nature of data distribution are the primary drivers of performance degradation. To address this, we propose a novel Federated Learning approach, "FedHetero," designed to adaptively adjust local training epochs based on communication delay and data volume imbalances. This adaptive strategy mitigates staleness without requiring the disclosure of private data statistics, offering a streamlined solution to enhance learning outcomes.

Individuals involved with the criminal justice system disproportionately experience mental health disorders. Drawing upon data from North Carolina courts covering 1994 to 2009, this study analyzes whether requiring offenders on probation to receive mental healthcare lowers their subsequent likelihood of reincarceration. By exploiting random variations in judge assignments, the analysis contrasts individuals mandated to participate in treatment programs with those under probation without such requirements. The findings reveal that mandating treatment reduces recidivism within three years by a margin of 5.6 percentage points—or 17 percent—compared to non-treatment probationers. While specific impacts on violent and property crimes demonstrate reduced recurrence, the beneficial trends also intensify as time progresses post-conviction. Finally, a cost-benefit assessment indicates that resulting decreases in crime sufficiently reimburse expenses associated with offering these programs.

Measuring atomic disorder levels is vital for understanding how changes in local structural environments influence material performance and longevity. This study utilizes graph neural networks to establish a physically grounded index for disorder severity, defined as the average distance from the most prevalent coordination pattern in the dataset. This approach highlights that significant shifts in local atomic arrangement—whether caused by thermal expansion or new phase creation—manifest as higher disorder levels. Findings demonstrate that this index highlights distinct transitions in the cubic zirconia to monoclinic transformation with emphasis on radiation damage and heating effects in aluminum, notably separating these events from the continuous changes associated with temperature variations.

The version of the proof format adopted by the veriT SMT solver was initially showcased ten years ago following the first PxTP workshop. Since its inception, this format has fully evolved to the point where it supports various SMT applications, with other proof-producing solvers also generating files in this format. To secure a better direction for future advancements in this format, this article aims to solicit input from practitioners. To achieve that, it will examine the evolution history of the format as well as the pragmatic strategies used through its development while discussing the issues that may arise when other generating-proofs engines rely on the veriT proofs format.

Synchronous updates often reduce efficiency in cross-device federated learning, specifically as the pool of active clients expands. Nguyen et al., 2022 demonstrated with their approach, dubbed FedBuff, that incorporating asynchronous updates alongside synchronous methods can mitigate this bottleneck. Their system assigns each participating device an asynchronous communication channel; however, this freedom introduces challenges regarding data consistency and the potential for malicious or unbalanced contributions. Our version of FedBuff addresses these issues through a commitment scheme that ensures both decentralised consistency and security. Furthermore, our adaptation maintains the original's performance benefits while remaining feasible when applied to existing communication channels.

Recent advances in automatic speech recognition (ASR) allow intermediates to map acoustic inputs, offering benefits for learning and inference. However, previously used intermediates were relatively complex and did not generalize well to various language models or speech generation models. This study explores the advantages of intermediate representations that are learned specifically to fit different downstream tasks. We introduce two approaches for achieving this: using intermediate representations as adaptable layers within a language model, and employing supervision during their learning. The resulting system achieves a 2.2 character error rate against humans on the English Turing test and also performs effectively in cross-lingual recognition when applied to German.

We introduce a Temporal Difference (TD) learning approach designed to tackle the navigation challenges marine robots encounter in underwater settings. To enhance data efficiency and ensure compatibility with real-time operations, the method integrates Gaussian Process regression with an advanced rejection-sampling algorithm for probability distribution generation. This allows the rejection-sampled, model-free ALGO to function as an model-based component, leveraging model-free predictions to create and train an integrated posterior distribution that accurately reflects the merged uncertainty from both sources. Numerical simulations and experiments conducted with an underwater vehicle demonstrate the approach's validity and practical effectiveness.

While most current Sequence-to-Sequence (Seq2Seq) Grammatical Error Correction (GEC) techniques primarily concentrate on generating extensive pseudo-training data to improve performance, very few tackle the challenge of few-shot domain adaptation. This study redefines various GEC environments as distinct tasks and introduces a methodology that applies few-shot meta-learning for domain adaptation entirely without synthetic pseudo data. By leveraging large data sets from source domains as anchors, we aim to create initial model parameters that enable rapid adaptation to new, low-resource target domains. Our approach specifically refines GEC capabilities across first languages (L1) acquired by learners developing non-native proficiency. Using nine diverse L1s as sources for meta-initialization and five additional L1s as target areas, we evaluate the system using an L1-specific adaptation corpus. Experimental results demonstrate that this method achieves a 0.50 point higher F_0.5 score compared to multi-task transfer learning baselines and allows for effective mastery of new domains using as few as 200 paired training instances.

The low surface brightness (LSB) spiral UGC 8839 typically exhibits very little stellar activity, yet it exhibits a surprising concentration of star formation along its outer edges. To investigate the mechanisms behind this off-axis activity, we conducted multi-wavelength observations ranging from gamma rays to radio waves, complemented by high-resolution hydrodynamic simulations. Comparing these datasets reveals that both the real data and simulation results exhibit the identical characteristic of outer-arm star formation; specifically, in UGC 8839, they localize in an "arm" significantly further out than where they appear in the standard simulation output. Interestingly, the simulation predicts that this shifted arm should not materialize in the actual galaxy, creating a clear discrepancy. Most crucially, both the model and observations for UGC 8839 correctly reproduce the spatial distribution of old stellar populations and the morphology of spiral density waves, features that were previously challenging to capture simultaneously in an LSB context. However, this success comes at a significant drawback regarding the physical conditions required to generate the gas shocks necessary to trigger star formation: while both the real galaxy and the baseline model correctly generate shocks and star formation at preferred locations, these now reach such extreme velocities that they threaten the structural stability of the galaxy. Conversely, our initial, unadjusted simulation model generated much weaker shock velocities, creating a more physically consistent scenario without compromising the spiral arm structure.

Pions serve as the dominant pseudo-Goldstone bosons arising from the spontaneous chiral symmetry breaking inherent to quantum chromodynamics (QCD). Their dynamics can be systematically modeled through chiral perturbation theory, which organizes interactions according to power counting schemes. However, the so-called chiral logarithm scheme proves insufficient for precision calculations in the non-relativisitic regime with large momentum where pions possess substantial binding energy and kinetic energy. To address these specific conditions, we introduce a novel effective theory known as relativistic composite Hype rforce theory (RCYT). This framework systematically expands pion amplitudes using an expansion based on the large four-momentum while retaining effective interactions derived from chiral logarithms. We demonstrate that this theory effectively accounts for crucial components of the relativistic expansion necessary to compute pion widths and scattering amplitudes with an accuracy corresponding to order p⁶ within the inductive counting theory (EPT) scheme.

Offline multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) focuses on learning effective multi-agent strategies from collected historical data, playing a crucial role in preparing systems for real-world deployment. A prevalent practical challenge is that individual behavior policies generating joint agent trajectories often exhibit varying performance levels—for instance, mixing a completely random policy with more competent medium-valued policies. In the context of cooperative games with global game states, we demonstrate that standard offline algorithms typically mistake agent-level data quality differences for game-state complexity, mistakenly directing training resources toward random policy experiences despite their low worth. To address this, we introduced "Offline Advantage Weighting with Action Correction" (O-WAC), a heuristic training approach designed to mitigate such biases. Evaluations across three benchmark tasks demonstrate that our method significantly enhances final team performance by giving appropriate emphasis to agent trajectories derived from higher-performing components.

In 1947, Fermi proposed a thought experiment designed to challenge the apparent instantaneous nonlocal implications of quantum mechanics. We offer fresh insights into this scenario by applying de Broglie-Bohm quantum trajectories alongside Heisenberg's uncertainty principle regarding the beam's transverse momentum. Our analysis clarifies the source of Einstein's anticipated absence of instantaneous effects and examines how they elevate to a macroscopic level. Specifically, we demonstrate through a practical example how these subtle global correlations, though insurmountable via quantum limitations, remain detectable through classical optical techniques.

**ABSTRACT**
Returning to Fermi's 1947 thought experiment, which aims to challenge the apparent instantaneous nonlocality of quantum mechanics, we propose a deeper analysis using de Broglie-Bohm trajectories and Heisenberg's uncertainty principle as applied to the target's initial transverse momentum. Our work clarifies why these global correlations, while truly instantaneous, manifest only macroscopically as very tiny effects and how they can be detected and potentially measured via standard classical optical techniques.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence and advanced information technology offers substantial benefits to the Internet of Vehicles (IoVs), yet it simultaneously introduces heightened security and privacy risks. Consequently, privacy preservation methods have become a primary area of research within IoVs, with Federated Learning emerging as a favored approach by generating model updates at edge nodes rather than transmitting raw data. Nevertheless, existing algorithms suffer from vulnerabilities due to attacks unauthenticated or malicious contributions from rogue IoVs. Furthermore, a lack of effective mechanisms exists to handle situations where IoVs decline participation after initial engagement. Addressing these gaps, this study proposes a secure framework for Federated Learning in IoVs equipped with a credible rejection mechanism. This proposal ensures a trustworthy and secure learning process by simultaneously preventing attacks from malicious nodes and facilitating the model upgrades of those who withdraw post-commitment.

We introduce a feedback encoding framework grounded in Gaussian mixture models (GMMs). Within this structure, GMM components define potential codewords, while mixing coefficients steer users toward specific code buckets aligned with channel states; consequently, mixing coefficients serve users uniquely, offering a distinct advantage over traditional scheme where entire mixing coefficient matrices are transmitted. Leveraging the low-dimensionality of channel states, we establish a theoretical framework demonstrating that the dominant error probability stems from users. To optimize this robustness against estimation mistakes, we formulate channel and user training as a joint design optimization centered on maximizing accuracy. Beyond standard design metrics, we introduce and analyze a user-centric optimization criterion essential for validating benefits over conventional methods. Numerical experiments confirm the proposed scheme significantly improves communication robustness relative to existing approaches.

Realistically, truly two-dimensional robust crosscurrents, defined by their flow perpendicular to usual extended eigenstates and conservation laws, have eluded detection despite prior predictions in ideal models. We confirm these robust currents in a 22-qubit system, encompassing both robustness against disturbances and resilience to defects within a 3D quantum lattice. A necessary condition for their stability in the face of defects is that the robust currents must remain exact even under spatial randomness. Additionally, we establish a sufficient condition: such currents must be "local," meaning they result from unitary transformations restricted to a small number of sites.

This paper examines physical layer security (PLS) within a dual-hop wireless system utilizing OFDM architectures. The research analyzes the distribution of the end-to-end secrecy rate for both series and parallel transmission protocols, considering uncorrelated additive white Gaussian noise across all subcarriers. To establish tractable bounds for the end-to-end secrecy rate, the authors derive lower limits for the cumulative distribution functions of two key random variables: the end-to-end legitimate channel capacity and the end-to-end eavesdropper channel capacity. These simplified functions serve as tight approximations, with analysis confirming that the end-to-end legitimate capacity exhibits a hyperexponential distribution, while the eavesdropper's follows a composite hyperexponential pattern. Text-based games provide an excellent framework for evaluating language comprehension, complex problem-solving, and common-sense inference in virtual agents, yet their performance remains constrained by legacy tooling, allowing only about 300 steps per second. We introduce TextWorldExpress, a high-performance version supporting three prominent game benchmarks that improves processing speed by a factor of 1,000, exceeding one million simulation steps per second off-the-shelf hardware. This dramatic boost cuts down computation times, allowing researchers to conduct experiments involving a billion states within roughly a day.

Long short-term memory (LSTMs) have established themselves as a de facto implementation of the recurrent neural network (RNN) architecture. The ever-increasing scale and complexity of datasets and applications necessitate corresponding expansions in model parameters, thereby raising concerns regarding the feasibility of deploying these systems across various infrastructures. To address this, researchers have focused on reducing model complexity without compromising accuracy. In this paper, we introduce the Linear LSTM, a novel architecture designed to mitigate the traditional linear dependencies within LSTM gates by utilizing fully connected layers instead. We demonstrate that the linearized components can be further optimized via low-ractor factorization without a significant drop in performance. Extensive evaluations across twelve diverse datasets spanning natural language processing (NLP) and time-series tasks reveal that the proposed Linear LSTMs consistently undercut both standard LSTMs and recent linear adaptations in both operational efficiency and parameter count, while maintaining superior or equivalent performance in tasks specific accuracy.

Saturn's stratosphere near its poles experiences the cyclical emergence and disappearance of extensive, warm vorticities located beyond approximately 75 degrees latitude, reaching maximum intensity during winter and completely disappearing throughout spring. The extended exploration period provided by the Cassini mission enabled scientists to analyze atmospheric changes with greater precision, revealing the spatiotemporal evolution of these features more accurately than prior to 2017). However, the full mechanism initiating this phenomenon on such an extreme axial tilt remains unexplained by both pre-Cassino observations and current analysis capabilities. To fill this gap, we have developed a high-resolution General Circulation Model (GCM) capable of simulating atmospheric processes across the entire range of Saturn's extreme axial tilt. This new model reproduces the observed broad (~3600 km) and warm feature near the Saturn pole with remarkable accuracy, an achievement the pre-Cassini GCM failed to accomplish even under optimized conditions based on single-satellite data. While the model performs well against multi-year Cassini measurements, certain constraints remain, such as simulating the extreme polar stratospheric temperatures recorded during the planet's 2018 equinox. We posit that the initial generation of this circular warmth anomaly is not driven by processes occurring within mid-latitudes—a leading hypothesis prior to the development of this new model—but originates locally within the polar region itself.

Spectroscopic techniques that rely on the spectral modification of a laser by matter capture both the phase and amplitude of its spectral density, offering amplitude and phase methods for extracting this combined information. This knowledge enables more reliable model testing and the identification of underlying physical processes. This paper introduces and demonstrates a model-independent algorithm to calculate these values directly from amplitude-based measurements, such as those produced by absorption, fluorescence, or phosphorescence. By applying this method to simulate and experimental data generated by absorption, fluorescence, and saturable upconversion, we confirm that accurate reconstruction of the phase spectrum is achievable for common linear and nonlinear optical phenomena, including the resulting shifts in line width and frequency. However, in the case of fluorescence, obstacles arising from the specific emission characteristics of emitting centers prevent successful calculation of the phase. Ultimately, findings underscore that while spectral amplitude is typically measured, neglecting these phases can introduce significant, sometimes critical, inaccuracies.

We also establish explicit bounds consistent with prior knowledge for specific applications, including low-density matrix recovery, graph nuclear norm minimization, and the graph master equation, all solved under fixed-rank constraints.

Ultimately, this research demonstrates the utility of non-agentic approaches and topological data in analyzing complex social phenomena illuminated only by partial information.

Precise and resilient localization represents a critical requirement for autonomous mobile entities. Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) methods, which integrate data from cameras, inertial units, and sometimes range finders or LiDAR, have recently garnered significant attention. However, existing solutions typically rely on standard assumptions, such as the necessity of visual features for every frame or limited reliance on frame rate, both of which can hinder deployment in many real-world scenarios. This paper examines several current VIO implementations and introduces a novel cloud-based, edge-supported visual-inertial navigation system that operates without these conventional constraints. Our developed system offers high localization accuracy while functioning with zero frame rate requirements, leveraging recent advancements in vision-free pose estimation APIs. Given the current scarcity of comparative studies on these specific technologies, this work also conducts targeted experiments to assess visual feature-free methods and integrates them effectively into the VIO framework. Ultimately, we have embedded these innovations into an extended open-source package, which has been rigorously validated through data from an actual field deployment on a real robot.

Quantum mechanics relies on linear equations, a constraint that ignores the potential significance of solutions arising from the non-linear operation of square-rooting. We relax this standard by treating field amplitudes as square roots, thereby enabling a scalar theory that is intentionally more non-linear. Within this framework, we introduce a square-root higher-order Weyl semimagnet model. This novel system lacks low-energy linearizations and does not employ the usual conservation of topology charges. Despite abandoning these specific traits, we identify it as a robust higher-order topology by demonstrating the emergence of mid-gap surface states on every crystallographic plane perpendicular to the "Wedgy" (or "Rogi") nodes found in the bulk. Because these states are localized on surfaces oriented internally to the material, they qualify as "quantum-chemical" or "body-surface" states. Crucially, their existence relies on the non-linear character of the model; they vanish if the higher-order topological invariants are neutralized through the non-linear combination of bulk modes, a scenario unattainable in traditional linear theories. As these collective states surpass those derived purely from boundary vacuum decay, we designate them for further study, highlighting both their distinctive physical properties and potential applications.

This article examines a data completion problem for time-harmonic Maxwell equations regarding the electric field within a bounded domain. Proofs are provided to establish the well-posedness, convergence, and regularity of the problem. Furthermore, after finite element discretization utilizing edge elements, diverse three- and two-dimensional numerical simulations demonstrate the method's efficacy, even when applied to data containing noise.

In this work, we investigate Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA), an approach designed to train a student model for a specific new task using contributions from multiple decentralized teacher models with distinct and self-contained prior training. This study addresses a current challenge in the model market, where a demand exists for a student model capable of performing optimally on a recent, specific task, synthesized from various distributed sources. The "selective" nature of FedSA is critical, as it incorporates weighted contributions from these teachers in a way that remains hidden during the process. While traditional federated learning methods focus on concealing the distribution of data, our approach specifically prioritRevealingly concealing the information regarding which distributed models are being contributed, and how significantly. This ensures that data owners retain full control, allowing them to decide voluntarily whether to share and precisely the extent of their parameter updates.

To validate the effectiveness of our method, we implemented it across both centralized and decentralized environments using three different scenarios. Our experiments demonstrate that this adaptive aggregation strategy successfully learns the new target task to the same level as a model trained without restrictions from data silos, without requiring knowledge of the source teachers or the volume of data they utilize. Ultimately, FedSA offers a viable solution for leveraging shared resources in a environment built on trust and decentralization.

The quantum null energy condition (QNEC) establishes a lower limit on the energy-momentum tensor, relating it to how the entanglement entropy of a sub-region varies along a null direction. Investigating the quantum thermodynamics of many-body systems within two spatial dimensions—specifically the fermionic ferromagnetic Heisenberg (FFH) model at finite temperature—we derive a novel "strong QNEC." This finding not only bounds the ffh tensor but also differentiates it by derivatives, utilizing the characteristics of maximally entangled states in many bodies and their connection to thermodynamic temperature. We also assess the validity of the qnec under varying regimes, including zero and non-zero magnetic states, as the system approaches its critical Curie point, and offer a general discussion on how maximally entangled geometry relates to thermodynamic concepts, such as temperature duality.

Our analysis reveals that as a parameter $\lambda$ approaches zero with $l_1$ coherence demonstrating non-trivial behavior for both a coherent state and the vacuum when applied to the Symanzik single-particle reduced density operator. Furthermore, we examine a particle in a magnetic field under a Keplerian potential; our calculations show the coherence non-trivial time dependence on field strength, which we use to establish the distinguishability time for initial and final qubit states.

Consider the $n$-dimensional unit cube $Q_n = [0,1]^n \subset \mathbb{R}^n$. Let $C(Q_n)$ represent the Banach space containing all continuous real-valued mappings on $Q_n$, equipped with the supremum norm defined as $\|f\|_{C(Q_n)} = \max_{x \in Q_n} |f(x)|$. For a specific function $f \in C(Q_n)$, its "rank" relative to a specific algebra $\mathcal{P}$ is the smallest integer $k$ such that $f$ can be expressed using at most $k$ elements from $\mathcal{P}$. When $\mathcal{P}$ consists of multivariate functions linear with respect to each variable separately (often known as circuit complexity), this measure aligns with that concept. The primary focus of this paper is to establish a sharp version of the Borsuk-Ulam theorem tailored to functions with low ranks within the algebra of functions formed by compositions. Specifically, for any such ranked function $f$, there exists a $(n-1)$-dimensional sphere centered at the origin within $\mathbb{R}^n$ upon which $\|f\|$ remains constant and strictly positive, a property that immediately yields significant outcomes regarding the topological structure of level sets.

Superconducting quantum circuits are recognized as a leading platform for quantum computing, yet material flaws within this technology currently dictate processing limits. Aligning with our ongoing effort to debug this hardware, we present a low-cost method to identify electrical defects in superconducting materials using a simple quantum capacitor circuit. Because radion frequency shifts caused by such imperfections occur in the micro range, we applied lock-in detection and spectral analysis to precisely measure these resonances. This affordable and high-resolution defect detection technique facilitates rapid quality control and assists in engineering more fault-tolerant quantum processors.

While Venus's current state remains uncertain, the research traces the progression from these massive eruptions through periods of chemical complexity and atmospheric cooling, ultimately analyzing the plausibility of Venus once harboring liquid water on its surface.

The resulting device, a **plasma-based optical phase plate (PS-WP)** formed by connecting two sulfur-capillary-filled tubes, successfully switches linear input light to circular output with over **98 percent** efficiency. Notably, this effect is independent of light wavelength. The underlying mechanism involves rapid thermal plasma creation in one fiber, inducing a current that passes through to the second fiber, creating a non-thermal skin-depth-thick plasma layer there. This skin-depth plasma alters the local index of refraction just enough to reach the **quarter-wave condition**, effectively turning the combination into an ultrafast, programmable waveplate capable of switching in less than a **microsecond**.

Building accurate automatic extraction models for visual-heavy documents, such as invoices, is significantly hampered by the expensive collection of thousands of well- annotated training samples required for robust performance. To address this, we present "Selective Labeling," which streamlines the annotation effort by requiring only binary "yes/no" confirmation for candidate extracts flagged by a model initially trained on sparsely labeled data. Merging this approach with a specialized active learning technique to identify instances where the model exhibits the highest uncertainty, we demonstrate via experiments across diverse domains (encompassing three specific document categories) that Selective Labeling lowers the cost of data labeling by a factor of ten while introducing minimal accuracy degradation.

Urban physical contacts and social networking are recognized drivers of cities' economic output, innovation, community resilience, and public health. Nevertheless, comprehensive, long-duration data on these activities at a comprehensive data scope have historically been lacking. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel approach for tracking the social anatomy of people across entire populations by synthesizing urban anonymous mobile data with internet-based social connection records. Applying this method to over 500,000 individuals in China reveals that face-to-face networking, while comprising a minor portion of daily routines, correlates strongly with economic performance across multiple metrics. Furthermore, our model can accurately reconstruct pre-pandemic social patterns from disrupted anonymous location information caused by COVID-19 restrictions.

In this work, we present the outcomes of our three-dimensional simulations examining viscous accretion onto sub-solar mass central stars within a massive molecular clump environment. The simulations resolve both gas and fully formed dust grains down to a Michaelis–Roberts (MR) magnetic breakdown threshold of 10 micrometers ($10^{-4}$ meters). Despite these refined conditions, our models still struggle to elevate low initial disc densities to the values required for bursts while developing within a cluster of massive stars. Naviging complex, dynamic indoor environments remains a significant challenge for autonomous mobile robots, particularly when deteriorating environmental conditions cause standard sensors to underperform and force reliance backup systems. Such failures often result in delayed obstacle detection, diminished detection ranges, and navigation errors. To proactively mitigate these issues, we developed a unified framework capable of identifying and adapting to the degradation of various sensors in real time. Our method estimates the level of deterioration for each specific modality, uses these metrics to dynamically adjust the parameters of the robot's existing algorithms, and further offers a mechanism to automatically swap out inferior systems without interruption. We validated this solution on a mobile platform using data from degraded cameras, LiDAR, and inertial units, demonstrating its efficacy through improved performance in both simulated and real-world indoor scenarios compared to baseline results using undamaged or static configurations of algorithms.

The issue of information security on social networks has become critical, particularly as companies like Facebook and Google struggle to effectively mitigate misinformation and invasive advertising. This research proposes a novel service provider model utilizing Game Theory to demonstrate that it can simultaneously achieve reliable safe-information dissemination and earn higher profits than traditional platforms. In this framework, traditional providers operate under an asymmetric information game, whereas novel "honest" entrants adopt a transparent signaling strategy. Findings indicate that these transparent vendors achieve signal equilibrium; moreover, Asymmetric Equilibrium within the conventional sector compels both social media giants and their users toward greater caution, enabling the proposed model to outperform legacy platforms in performance metrics and financial outcomes. Consequently, this study not only offers a path for enhancing public information ecosystems but also positions social media corporations more responsibly.

The problem involves estimating the parameters of a one-dimensional Gaussian random field (GRF) from a set of data points. Each data point is defined by a visible parameter vector and a corresponding latent parameter. The visible vectors create a function mapping these points to the latent dimension by associating each point with its k-nearest neighbors in the latent space using a specific regression. Within this study, the latent regression function is modeled as a sparse linear combination of kernel functions evaluated at distinct "source locations," which are determined simultaneously during estimation. A nonparametric approach is employed, utilizing a Fisher information matrix to assess the density of the data's kernel-based manifold and selecting kernel parameters based on this density assessment to ensure a well-fitted model. The paper concludes by demonstrating this methodology through numerical experiments and various real-world applications.

Addressing outliers and noise pollution from contaminated data, $\ell_1$-norm principal component analysis ($\ell_$-PCA)) has emerged as a robust alternative to the standard methods of PCA. However, the optimization required for $\l_$-PCA) is non-convex and generally unyielding to direct resolution. In this paper, we introduce a novel, efficient algorithm to resolve this challenge. Our approach leverages a specific algebraic property: the projection of a rank-$d$ matrix onto the $\l_1$) unit ball can be expressed as the optimal solution to a specific, constrained quadratic formulation. Relying on this characterization, our proposed technique replaces general, black-box numerical solvers with direct linear system equations tailored for computing each component of the approximation sequence during iterative progress through descent steps over the non-smooth gradient orientation. Experiments indicate this strategy not only matches but frequently surpasses $\l_1$) PCA) in both accuracy and execution time across a spectrum of scenarios including image dimension reduction.

Annotated data are traditionally utilized to input supervised machine learning, yet expensive labels (such as those derived from expert knowledge) often pose a significant cost barrier. To address this, Unger et al. (2018) recently proposed using automatic label generation via neural language models to facilitate cheaper labels. In the current work, we apply this framework to enhance annotations of dialog behavior within a conversational voice assistant. Specifically, we analyze whether the BERT neural language model effectively identifies existing semantic and pragmatic structures in labels assigned to dialog act tags. Our results demonstrate that multi-label classification using BERT achieves superior label performance compared to single-label constraints, suggesting that similar labeling strategies could benefit other tasks involving semantic or pragmatic datasets.

Autonomous navigation within unfamiliar environments is crucial for mobile robots, requiring that maps serve as the foundational element. While most existing representations depend on global metric maps, maintaining and managing them is often too demanding for resource-constrained robots operating in vast areas. Although maintaining a global uncertainty map (GUM) offers a promising middle ground by balancing global and local information, its application to large areas remains non-trivial due to the integration challenges associated with data from varying levels of uncertainty. We introduce the Robotic GUM (RGUM), a framework designed to preserve and manage a GUM specifically to autonomously navigate large, unknown environments. Our framework partitions the global GUM into several smaller, well-uncertained local maps. We estimate the spatial transformation between these units using a method that accounts for map-unspecific uncertainty, which helps keep the overall GUM intact. Furthermore, we define a transition to split or merge these local blocks only when necessary, ensuring efficient preservation and management of the global map. Experiments conducted on both a real robot and a simulated platform confirm that our approach effectively maintains GUMs and successfully guides navigation across large, unknown spaces.

Object-Oriented programming languages typically rely heavily on dynamic memory allocation. Consequently, high-performance computing (HPC) frameworks often optimize this process using specialized allocators that surpass the capabilities of standard language runtimes. Despite the widespread availability of these tools for parallel execution environments, there has not been a general approach to create consistent, top-tier performers for serial (single-threaded) tasks.

Our investigation reveals that these parallel memory allocators excel due to multiple internally developed components. A critical, yet overlooked, factor driving this high achievement is their use of highly optimized, domain-specific sequential codebases. We advocate the concept of Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO)—comprising one executed function across numerous distinct programs (C++ "classes" and "instances"). This paradigm stands apart from Multi-Program One-Distributed-Memory (MPO), which is common in traditional supercomputing using several sequential programs running on a single many-threaded many-threaded node.

In this paper, we detail how this STMO (or just MO if you want to keep it more general) execution model allows for the creation of extremely efficient, parallel memory allocation systems tailored for serial processes. By sharing these implementations, we aim to contribute to the ecosystem. The results indicate that these sequential libraries significantly outperform both OpenMP multi-threaded modules and OpenACC multi-gpu modules in terms of both memory allocation speed and overall program runtime.

We compute the nonequilibrium current and noise in a symmetric Josephson junction, where each side contains a separate magnetic impurity located on a single-layered, d-wave superconducting material in a out-of-phase state. By utilizing a noise-assisted tunneling framework within the nonequilibrium Green's function approach, we demonstrate the feasibility of distinguishing individual YSR levels and their splitting behaviors. Specifically, impurities associated with unit splitting exhibit noise characteristics indicative of equilibrium conditions, whereas those with reduced or un-solden splitting display nonequilibrium features. Since impurity positioning determines splitting, this finding enables accurate locus finding. Furthermore, because noise continuum interactions vary based on whether impurity-induced states lie above or below the chemical potential, these results offer a method to detect nonequilibrium contributions to contoured spectral gaps, which serve as confirmation of the d-wave ordering. Ultimately, a skewet tunneling parameter facilitates equilibrium measurements to capture these nonequilibrium signatures, thereby validating the presence of d-wave superconductivity in monolitic materials through noise analysis.

This study investigates the electronic and magnetic properties of interstitial and substituted impurities of Nitrogen and Carbon within rutile TiO₂. We specifically focus on the substitutional phase, challenging the existing paradigm that treats this phase as non-magnetic. Our findings, which align with recent experimental data, reveal both carbon and nitrogen in substitutional positions exhibit d⁰ ferromagnetism. However, the underlying mechanism differs: nitrogen substitution induces a symmetry-breaking lattice distortion, whereas occupying a carbon atom results in a symmetric structure. Furthermore, analyzing various interstitial sites indicates that inserting these atoms into the 4b site is most favorable energetically for both, as it simultaneously offers the lowest formation energy and the greatest magnitude of magnetization. Consequently, previous experiments observing strong ferromagnetism in interstitial-doped TiO₂ can now be explained by the coexistence of uncompensated spins. We support these conclusions through first-principles calculations, detailed electronic structure analysis, and a detailed magnetic picture.

Although the ability to produce highly relativistic electron-positron pairs with significant circular polarization in laser-solid interactions is well-established, the polarization characteristics of positons have received far less attention. Using the quantum electrodynamics (QED) cascade formalism, this study examines the causes and ranges of positon polarization under strong-field conditions. Findings indicate that while normal and transverse laser fields can indeed yield highly rounded posons with strong transverse spin, both normal and transverse driving fields influence the polarization level. Furthermore, the average spin orientation of the resulting posons shifts significantly with the incidence angle of the laser, varying from 0.3 to 0.9. The reduction in poson polarization is also attributed to the temperature of the driven electron plasma, as well as the normal component of the laser intensity. Finally, the study offers insight into the mechanisms affecting poson polarization across diverse strong-field parameters.

This study investigates the stationary fingering instability of an elastic membrane dividing two fluids with differing densities within a rotating container. By applying an energy approach, we derive a variational problem whose solutions identify the most unfavorable initial perturbations free of horizontal wavenumber. Subsequent incorporation of specific initial perturbations allows us to determine the single optimal wavenumber, whose associated perturbation triggers the onset of fingering. Elasticity and rotational forces suppress pattern formation in the high-gravity, high-stiffness, or low-tension limits; however, there exists a non-zero range of parameters where these competing effects produce distinct structures unobserved in simpler scenarios. This behavior persists whether surface tension effects are included or ignored, suggesting that both rigorous energy-based predictions and experimental setups could yield novel, rotation-induced patterns that account for material elasticity.

These data reach a column density sensitivity of $4.0 \times 10^{18} \, \text{cm}^{-2}$ for $C_6HCH$, consistent with previously reported values for ethynyl benzene in Orion KL. Given this sensitivity, a source exhibiting a column density of $10^{22} \, \text{cm}^{-2}$ would yield a $6\sigma$ signal; consequently, $C_6HCC$ should be readily identifiable in any methanol maser-associated star-forming outflows.

The discrepancy advancing between biological research breakthroughs and actual patient health improvements catalyzed the field of translational medicine, ensuring that integrating new knowledge into our healthcare system is equally vital as its initial discovery. Organizations such as the National Institute of Health (NIH) subsequently adopted the term, which has since permeated biomedical education and professional discourse throughout society. However, critics argue that "translation" implies an inevitable process, potentially masking required policy shifts and funding strategies. Although concepts like "translational research," "research translation," and "applying research" are functionally identical, these words lack the ideological baggage associated with "translation." Consequently, this paper proposes replacing "translation" with "application" in future conversations, aiming to preserve the phrase's utility as a unifying label while eliminating restrictive conceptions and false assumptions.

We examine a coherent dissipative dark fluid framework that incorporates both dissipative and undissipative undulations. In this model, dissipative behavior constitutes the primary aspect, while both membrane theory and causal hydrodynamics serve as constitutive relations for the fluid. Our analysis reveals that the model effectively mimites $\Lambda$CDM when the Caullus hydrodynamic approach is used, though it exhibits distinct features under different scenarios. Specifically, the undissipative wave mode functions as an equation of state modifier, influencing the apparent dark energy equation of state within the Attractor theory context. Furthermore, we observe that the Dunnex and other dark energy models can emerge from this unified dissipative structure. The density parameters derived from bulk and elastic viscous processes, when integrated into our model, successfully reproduce $\text{qcdm}$ models, including those proposed by Dunnex and others. Our work involves numerical simulations exploring the model's dynamical system, calculations of the potential, and analyses of its stability.

This paper investigates the implications of $J/\psi$ decays into undetectable states, focusing on light sterile neutrinos and dark matter (DM) with masses below the GeV scale. We employ low-energy Effective Field Theories to model both scenarios, using current experimental limits on invisible $J/\psi$ decays to derive robust constraints on neutrino and neutrino interaction parameters, as well as specific couplings involving long-lived neutralinos. Additionally, we address recent findings from the BESIII collaboration regarding the $\Upsilon(4S)$ decay into a $J/\psi$ and two photons, applying these results to refine bounds on sterile neutrino physics. Collectively, our work significantly narrows the permissible parameter spaces for sub-GeV dark matter and light sterile neutrinos, guiding future high-precision measurements.

This study establishes Multivariate Functional Singular Spectrum Analysis (MFSSA), the functional extension capable of operating across diverse dimensional domains for multivariate Singular Spectrum Analysis (MSSA). We present the comprehensive theoretical underpinnings required for the research alongside the implementation framework and algorithmic strategies. Through empirical simulation, we demonstrate that the MFSSA method achieves superior reconstruction accuracy when processing multivariate functional time series (MFTS) compared to existing techniques. Additionally, a applied analysis utilizing multivariate functional time series temperature data from the GFS global weather model effectively highlights the method's utilities. The combined theoretical, simulative, and practical outcomes provide a robust basis for applying MFSSA in practical scenarios involving multivariate functional time series data.

We demonstrate the power law decay $p(t, \gamma) \sim t^{-\delta}$, where $p(t, \gamma)$ represents the probability that a continuous-time random walk on $\Z_{\ge 0}$ at time $t$ has position $\le -\gamma t$. This result is established by determining the spectral bounds of the truncated operator $H_{-\gamma t}$ and applying these spectra as both upper and lower estimates for $p(t, \gamma)$. Furthermore, we prove an equivalent equivalence: $p(t, \gamma)$ equals the $(2+\alpha)$-th power law in $t$ for some exponent $\alpha > 0$. Additionally, the maximal position of the walk over the interval $[0,t]$ exhibits asymptotic behavior of order $t^{(\alpha+1)/(\alpha+2)}$.

The development of novel plasma components requires tunable high-current devices. This study introduces the design, fabrication, and evaluation of a Helicon Plasma Source (HPS), characterized by a coaxial inductively coupled architecture. The unique feature of this HPS lies in its magnet system, composed of two independent coils: one surrounding the chamber responsible for confining the skin layer plasma, and a second, inner coil situated inside the reaction vessel to generate a strong local magnetic field, thereby inducing a metastable state known as double skin layer or "helicon" discharge mode. During testing, the device successfully sustained a 20 Ampere current, with the helicon transition observed between 14 and 21 Ampere. Spatial measurements indicate a radial confinement of approximately 1.2 cm, while electron density reached around $10^{13} \text{cm}^{-3}$, validated by microwave interferometry. These results offer a pathway for creating plasma components suitable for inertial fusion support, magnetic confinement applications, and advanced material processing.

Although automated nucleus segmentation supports early cancer diagnosis, developing fully supervised models is hindered by the lack of data and the high cost and time required for annotation. While weak supervision techniques utilizing only search prompts like crop pairs or crop queries offer a viable solution, they remain vulnerable to biases and inconsistencies often found in such annotations, which can severely degrade segmentation performance. To address this, we introduce Nucleus Segmentaion with Augmented supervision using Nucleus detection (NuASeAN), a framework designed to leverage both detection results and segmentation prompts trained on a network with partial parameter sharing. This approach integrates the detection task with the segmentation task to effectively leverage the complementary strengths of both. To validate the method, we evaluate NuASeAN on the Prostate Segmentation Challenge (ProstateSeg) dataset; its strong results demonstrate that the method effectively mitigates weaknesses typically associated with weak supervision. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/zhenghuawei/NuASeAN.

Although Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) serve as the predominant architecture for processing graph-structured data, their high number of hyperparameters often poses a barrier, especially in noniterative data annotation scenarios. To address this, we introduce Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), a streamlined variant that eliminates hyperparameter iteration entirely by utilizing convolution filters initialized with random values and adapting them through backpropagation. Because this design requires no other parameter tuning efforts, it offers a straightforward, automated approach. As a proof of the method's viability, we defined nine clinical conditions—such as pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, and COVID-19 based on medical input—and achieved results radiographically indistinguishable from real images (FID $\approx$ 18.9). Since none of the trained examples included actual pathogens, the generated model itself produces no images showing signs of infection. Finally, while the technique was specialized for chest X-rays to keep the task manageable, the authors argue its principles can be extended to other medical imaging modalities.
